_comment: Synthetic, redistributable transcript for the public test suite. Three 90s windows: two carry investor-lens signal (unit economics, moats, capital allocation, margins), one is off-topic chatter. Real show transcripts live in the private fixtures repo.

segments.text: Welcome back, today we are talking with an operator who has run three software companies.
Let's start with the business model shift you saw last year.
The unit economics changed completely once inference costs fell by an order of magnitude.
Gross margins went from forty percent to seventy percent in two quarters.
That cost curve is the mechanism, and it is falsifiable: watch the margins next quarter.
Competitors without pricing power will feel it first, and their moats were thin to begin with.
So the competitive dynamics reward whoever controls distribution, not whoever has the best model.
Capital allocation follows: the incumbents are buying back stock instead of funding the transition.
Management incentives explain that; their comp is tied to earnings per share, not market structure.
And the balance sheet decisions they make this year decide who survives the re-pricing.
Which is a base-rate-defying claim, so let me give you the mechanism and the number.
Anyway, before we go deeper, funny story from the green room earlier.
The host spilled coffee on the producer and everyone laughed for five minutes.
We talked about the weather, a celebrity wedding, and which restaurant has the best tacos.
Somebody's cousin knows the drummer from that band, which was the drama of the week.
Then we argued about whether pineapple belongs on pizza, which it does not.
None of this matters for the show, but it was a good time.
Okay, back to it. What about regulation as a catalyst?
The policy change re-prices the whole industry because it changes who bears the compliance cost.
Pricing power moves to the two players with the licenses, and everyone else becomes a price taker.
That market structure is the moat now, and the regulatory catalyst created it overnight.
So my falsifiable claim: their margins expand by ten points within four quarters or I am wrong.
Labor is the other cost curve; AI compresses the analyst layer and that shows up in operating margins.
Capital allocation again decides it: the ones reinvesting the savings win the next decade.
